# Base scale and phase: exact affine-interval depth and an interior minimum ridge

This note studies the actual deformation (z,x) -> (s z+t,x), s>0,
while the sampled lattice remains Z times R. It is different from the
fixed-base fiber translations in `candidate 8bccfe18db0ced3d`
and from the one-fiber replacements in
`candidate fd2a9bc72f818ad3`.

There is an exact interior local minimum with three positive sampled
fibers. It is strict when either scale or phase alone is varied, but
is a flat ridge in the full two-parameter space. That ridge can reach
positive-width support contact. It cannot continue through a change
of sampled-fiber count without increasing maximal normalized depth.
Thus support contact and non-increasing support deletion are distinct.

All maxima below are over every actual mixed-integer point and every
closed ambient halfspace. They are not just own-centroid evaluations.

## 1. Why the continuous midpoint is optimal in each fiber

After a permitted continuous affine shear, every affine interval roof
has fibers centered at x=0. Reflection (z,x) -> (z,-x) preserves the
source measure and sends every halfspace to a halfspace. Therefore
the depth at (j,x) equals that at (j,-x).

Depth superlevel sets are convex: any halfspace containing a convex
combination of two points contains at least one of the two points,
so its mass is at least the smaller of their depths. Consequently
the depth at (j,0) is at least the depth at every (j,x) in that fiber.
The global maximum is exactly the maximum of the finitely many
midpoint depths. This uses the actual reflection symmetry; it is not
an own-midpoint rule for arbitrary interval families.

Let the positive widths at bases 0,...,N-1 be w_k. A nonvertical cap
through (j,0), with one orientation, has mass

    F_j(beta)=sum_k clamp(w_k/2+beta(k-j),0,w_k),          (1)

where clamp(v,0,w)=min(w,max(0,v)). The other orientation gives the
same set of masses by reflection. Every vertical through-cap has
at least the mass of one of the finite, sufficiently steep caps in
(1): it contains the full boundary fiber, whereas that cap contains
half. Thus inf_beta F_j(beta) is the exact absolute midpoint depth.

## 2. A finite exact formula for every affine width profile

Reverse the base if necessary. For nonconstant affine widths, divide
by their common positive increment and write

    w_k=q+k,  q>0,  0<=k<N.

Define the two outer, eventually constant cap values

    E_j^- =sum_(i<j)(q+i)+(q+j)/2,
    E_j^+ =sum_(i>j)(q+i)+(q+j)/2.

For k!=j define

    T_(j,k)(q)=
      sum_(i<k) min(q+i,(k-i)(q+j)/(2(k-j))),    k>j;
      sum_(i>k) min(q+i,(i-k)(q+j)/(2(j-k))),    k<j.      (2)

All indices in these sums lie in 0,...,N-1. Then the exact absolute
and normalized global depths are

    D_j(q)=min(E_j^-,E_j^+, {T_(j,k)(q): k!=j}),
    A_N(q)=max_(0<=j<N) D_j(q),
    beta_N(q)=A_N(q)/[Nq+N(N-1)/2].                      (3)

For N=1 the set of T-values is empty and D_0=q/2.

Here is a complete proof of the finite reduction. The function (1)
is continuous, piecewise affine, and constant outside a finite
interval. At an event where a trace becomes empty its derivative
jumps upwards; at an event where a trace becomes full it jumps
downwards. Hence a minimum is achieved at an outer constant value
or at an event where at least one trace is empty. A flat minimum
interval has such an endpoint unless it reaches an outer constant
region. Simultaneous events cause no problem: if there is no empty
trace event, a nonzero downward jump cannot begin an interior
minimum. The event making trace k empty is

    beta=-(q+k)/(2(k-j)).

At this slope the unclipped mass in trace i is exactly

    (k-i)(q+j)/(2(k-j)).

It is positive precisely for i<k when k>j, or i>k when k<j.
Clipping at the full width gives (2), proving (3).

Each D_j is a concave, piecewise affine function of q with rational
coefficients. Indeed each T-value is a sum of minima of affine
functions, and a finite minimum of concave functions is concave.
The maximum A_N remains piecewise affine, but need not be concave.
It follows that beta_N is piecewise linear-fractional with a finite
set of rational breakpoints. On a piece with A_N(q)=alpha q+eta,
its derivative is

    [alpha*N(N-1)/2-N*eta]/[Nq+N(N-1)/2]^2.              (4)

Thus there is no isolated differentiable interior stationary minimum
within one affine piece: the sign is fixed, or the quotient is
constant there. All nonflat local minima occur at the explicitly
enumerable rational events in (2)-(3), including changes of the
maximizing base. This is an exact finite classification procedure
for every N, not a claim that those minima occur only at support loss.

For zero increment, the widths are all equal. The exact normalized
maximum is 1/2 for odd N and (N-1)/(2N) for even N. At base j a
symmetric block of 2min(j,N-1-j)+1 fibers gives the lower bound,
and a sufficiently steep cap gives the matching upper bound.

## 3. Exact three-fiber formula and its strict ratio minimum

For a convenient affine parametrization take widths

    (q,q+2,q+4),  q>0.

The endpoint midpoint depths are q/2 and (q+4)/2, since the other
fibers can be excluded by a finite tilt. At the middle midpoint,
retain the whole middle interval and centered subintervals of length
q at both endpoints. This is a symmetric submeasure of mass 3q+2,
so every containing cap has mass at least (3q+2)/2. The cap slope
beta=-(q+4)/2 in (1) captures the whole left fiber, half the middle,
and zero length on the right, attaining this bound. Section 1 shows
that these midpoint maxima are the full per-fiber maxima. Therefore

    beta_3(q)=max(q+4,3q+2)/(6q+12)
      =(q+4)/[6(q+2)],       0<q<=1;
       (3q+2)/[6(q+2)],      q>=1.                      (5)

Its derivatives on the two branches are respectively

    -1/[3(q+2)^2],  2/[3(q+2)^2].

It has a unique strict minimum at q=1, of value 5/18. This is the
profile (1,3,5). Equivalently, for endpoint width ratio r=a/b<=1,
the minimizing ratio is r=1/5. The formula is consistent with
`candidate 5048c7e97ca98aef`; here its role under base
scale and phase, and its support-boundary behavior, are different.

## 4. One fixed body and an interior scale-phase ridge

Fix the full planar convex trapezoid

    C={ (z,x): -1/4<=z<=9/4, |x|<=(1+2z)/2 }.

All its real fibers have strictly positive length, ranging from
1/2 to 11/2. Apply (z,x) -> (s z+t,x). The transformed projection
is [t-s/4,t+9s/4]. In the open chamber

    -1<t-s/4<0,  2<t+9s/4<3,                            (6)

the actual sampled bases are exactly 0,1,2. Their widths are

    (q,q+2,q+4)/s,  q=s-2t>0.

The common continuous scaling 1/s cancels from normalized depth,
so (5) is exact throughout this chamber. In particular (s,t)=(1,0)
is an interior local minimum. At fixed phase t=0 it is strict in s;
at fixed scale s=1 it is strict in t. In the full plane the entire
minimum set in (6) is the ridge

    t=(s-1)/2,  10/11<s<14/11.                          (7)

The fixed ambient trapezoid has extra real-base portions outside the
convex hull of its three sampled fibers. No identity C=conv(C intersect
(Z times R)) is assumed. At each parameter, replacing the body by
the convex hull of its entire sampled set preserves every sampled
fiber and all the depths computed here; however, performing that hull
replacement at every step would be a different deformation from the
specified affine images of one fixed body.

The flat direction is genuine. Thus this example is not an isolated
two-parameter local minimum and does not prevent reaching support
contact along a constant-depth path.

## 5. What happens at the two ends of the ridge

At s=10/11,t=-1/22 the upper projection endpoint is 2. The fiber
at base 2 still has positive width and is retained, because the
source body and halfspaces are closed. The sampled widths remain
proportional to (1,3,5), so the value at this boundary point is 5/18.
Immediately across this boundary the last fiber disappears with
positive limiting width. The remaining profile tends to (1,3),
whose exact maximum depth is 3/8. It is strictly larger than 5/18.

At s=14/11,t=3/22 the upper projection endpoint reaches 3. The new
fiber is already present at that parameter, with positive width.
The four widths are proportional to (1,3,5,7), and their exact
per-fiber midpoint depths are

    (1/2,5/2,13/2,7/2).

Consequently the global normalized value at entrance is 13/32,
again strictly larger than 5/18. Here is a short all-cap certificate
for the only new nontrivial value, 13/2 at base 2. For beta>=0,
the paired fibers at bases 1 and 3 in (1) contribute at least 5;
with the own half-length 5/2 this already exceeds 13/2. For
beta=-v<=0, if v<=1/4 those paired fibers still contribute 5.
If v>=1/4 the base-0 fiber is fully captured and contributes 1,
and the base-1/base-3 pair always contributes at least 3. Adding
the own half-length 5/2 gives at least 13/2. Equality is attained
at beta=-7/2. Base 1 retains the preceding (1,3,5) submeasure and
has a matching cap beta=-5/2 excluding the fourth fiber. The exposed
endpoints have their ordinary half-length depths.

For an explicit finite global upper cover, use for each base j the
cap x<=beta_j(z-j) and its x-reflection, where

    (beta_0,beta_1,beta_2,beta_3)=(-7/2,-5/2,-7/2,7/2).

Each pair covers its full fiber, and each cap has at most 13/2 mass.
This verifies the global upper bound at every candidate, including
boundary points; the midpoint lower certificates give equality.

Any continuous parameter path starting inside the ridge and remaining
at normalized depth at most 5/18 must stay on q=1 as long as it has
these three samples, by (5). The only exits of that ridge from the
chamber are the two points just analyzed. The entrance point itself
has larger depth. The positive-width loss point has a neighborhood
on the two-sample side with depth strictly larger than 5/18, by its
explicit continuous two-fiber formula. Motion along the boundary
with a different q also raises the three-fiber depth. Thus no such
path can pass through a change of sampled-fiber count. It can reach
the positive-width loss contact, but cannot continue through it
without raising the objective.

This is a local deformation obstruction, above the sharp target 1/4.
It does not exhibit a below-target body or a global minimizer over
all convex bodies. It also does not rule out deformations other
than base scale and phase.

## 6. Zero-width loss is a different boundary

An affine roof may instead vanish at a projection endpoint. In that
case a sample entering or leaving at that endpoint has limiting
mixed mass zero. Provided the remaining total mass stays positive,
the normalized maximum is continuous through this event. Formula
(1), or the full finite breakpoint formula including zero widths,
gives continuous depths on the retained bases. The new endpoint's
own maximum is half its vanishing width, since it is exposed.
Hence its candidate cannot create a jump. This argument does not
apply to the positive-width projection endpoints in Sections 4-5.

The exact verifier
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_base_scale_phase_affine_interval_depth.py` checks all cap
breakpoints against (2)-(3), the three-fiber formula, both boundary
profiles, the ridge inequalities and the finite four-fiber cap cover.
